sources.d_short: A fleet average; no loop shapes or machine code
sources.differs: A fleet average on production workloads; the post does not say whether the 0.30% includes PGO, a toolchain version or a hardening mode; no per-loop breakdown, machine code or controls a stranger can rerun. This study tests none of its numbers.
sources.m_short: An average 0.30% across Google’s services; PGO further improved performance
sources.measured: As reported: an average 0.30% performance impact across Google’s services; fixing one unnecessary check took the overhead from 0.35% to 0.3%; PGO further improved performance, though the overhead remains minimal even without such techniques; a handful of performance-critical code paths still use explicitly unsafe accesses.
sources.name: Google Security Blog, Nov 15 2024

sources.d_short: The same fleet; PGO tested here only with the timed input as training
sources.differs: The same fleet, with its method; no loop shapes. This study’s one PGO test (training input equal to the timed input, one CPU model) did not make the cost vanish in most rows; its census (the expensive shape is rare in general code) is consistent with few unsafe sites, a link not tested here.
sources.m_short: PGO critical; five services opted out; the unsafe-access API used in seven places
sources.measured: As reported, read in a browser (its address returned HTTP 403 to a scripted fetch when re-checked, so the figures are not confirmed from a saved copy): key services were benchmarked; PGO was critical, letting the compiler move checks out of hot paths; only five services opted out entirely; the fine-grained unsafe-access API was used in just seven distinct places; a non-verbose mode cut the binary-size cost from 2% to under 0.5%.
sources.name: Dionne, Rebert, Shavrick, Varlamov, “Practical Security in Production: Hardening the C++ Standard Library at Massive Scale”, ACM Queue 23(5), 2025

sources.differs: This study’s PGO column trains on the timed input, so it tests his PGO point only in part (it did not make the cost vanish in most rows on one CPU model); its loops are the cases where the check stays inside the loop.
sources.measured: An expert account, not a measurement. As reported: credits LLVM’s check optimization and PGO; says without PGO the overhead would not be tolerable for most performance-sensitive workloads; warns that benchmarks of pervasive patterns skew toward confirmation bias.
sources.name: Chandler Carruth, “Story-time: C++, bounds checking, performance, and compilers”, Nov 2024

sources.d_short: Rust; layout not controlled, here it is
sources.differs: Rust, many real benchmarks, several machines. As reported, it attributes checks-make-it-faster results to code layout and inlining heuristics without controlling layout; this study controls layout on eight C++ loops.
sources.m_short: 76.4% of benchmarks of top Rust crates pay little, nothing or less
sources.measured: As reported: 76.4% of benchmarks of top Rust crates show little, no or negative cost from unchecked indexing; 23.6% are more than 1% slower with checks and 11.8% more than 1% faster; brotli’s overhead 7.7%, 6.5% on an older rustc, 2.5% on Apple M1; about 200 benchmarks with 95% intervals.
sources.name: Popescu, Xu, Apostolakis, August, Levy, “Safer at Any Speed” (NADER), OOPSLA 2021

sources.d_short: One forward shape; vectorization not analysed
sources.differs: A dedicated machine with frequency scaling off and a far tighter interval, but one forward shape and an old compiler. Forward loops cost little here too; the shapes that lose SIMD are what it did not test.
sources.m_short: vector.at(i) 0.881% slower on sequential writes (GCC 4.6.2, a PC with two Xeon X5450 CPUs)
sources.measured: As reported: GCC 4.6.2 on a PC with two Xeon X5450 CPUs (a Dell Precision T5400) under Linux, with Turbo Boost unsupported, frequency scaling left out of the kernel and SpeedStep off, 63 runs per cell; vector.at(i) 0.881% (±0.009) slower than a C array at -O3; sequential write loops only; vectorization not analysed.
sources.name: Flater and Guthrie (NIST), “A Case Study of Performance Degradation Attributable to Run-Time Bounds Checks on C++ Vector Access”, J. Res. NIST 118, 2013

sources.d_short: A whole program; no intervals or controls
sources.differs: A whole real program with every check removed; no intervals, A/A or machine code. This study times loops, not a whole program.
sources.m_short: Every check removed from one Rust program: within the noise
sources.measured: As reported: a rustc patched to drop every bounds check; 1,227 checks per warm read; results well within the noise threshold; no hardware or run count stated.

summary: Google’s post reports an average 0.30% performance impact across its services, and says profile-guided optimization (PGO) improved performance further. Its 2025 sequel in ACM Queue, as reported (read in a browser; scripted fetches get HTTP 403, so unconfirmed from a copy), calls PGO critical. The closest per-benchmark study, NADER (OOPSLA 2021, on Rust), reports little, no or negative cost from unchecked indexing in 76.4% of benchmarks, and NIST (2013) vector.at(i) 0.881% slower than a C array on sequential writes. As reported, link order and environment size can reverse a measured speedup (Mytkowicz et al., 2009), hence the aligned build and the layout A/A here.
